title: User interface design in video games (Game Developer)
label: practitioner
claim: Summarises Fagerholt & Lorentzon taxonomy: diegetic/meta/spatial/non-diegetic along two axes (in fiction? in game geometry?). Advice: non-diegetic is the fallback when other forms hurt legibility or consistency; diegetic UI can frustrate when not legible in world geometry.

title: Hodent masterclass listing / Gamer's Brain
label: snippet
claim: Hodent splits game UX into usability (ease of use within human perception/attention/memory limits) and engage-ability (motivation, emotion, game flow). A game can be easy to use and still boring.

title: Idle-game UI growth search results
label: snippet
claim: Idle devs report trimming unused side panels (Miner 2149 devlog), hiding sections until thresholds, and players asking to see upcoming unlock goals to plan; a locked-unlock requirement not matching real appearance confused a player.

title: Game Accessibility Guidelines, Basic tier
label: guideline
claim: Basic tier includes: large well-spaced interactive elements esp. on touch; easily readable default font size; high contrast text/UI vs background; no essential info by fixed colour alone; no essential info by sound alone; progress through text prompts at own pace; start game without multiple menu levels; all UI reachable with the gameplay input method; remap controls; save all settings; simple clear language; avoid flicker. No numeric sizes given.

title: Hoober 2013 (full fetch)
label: research
claim: Field observation: one-handed 49%, cradled 36%, two-handed 15% (90% portrait). Grip changes often, sometimes every few seconds, by task. Author's later comment: people touch the centre of the screen; ignore the reach drawings. No target sizes given.

title: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)
label: guideline
claim: Targets at least 24x24 CSS px, or smaller if a 24px circle centred on each does not intersect another target. Stricter 2.5.5 recommended for important controls. Apple 44pt and Material 48dp were NOT verified from primary pages (fetch returned empty).

title: WCAG 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus
label: guideline
claim: Hover/focus-revealed content must be dismissible, hoverable, persistent. Says nothing about touch, where hover does not exist.

title: Into the Breach design postmortem (GDC 2019, Matthew Davis)
label: snippet
claim: Talk listing only. Reviews (not developer) say enemy intents are all shown and outcomes previewed before commitment: perfect information, small numbers.

title: A Dark Room critical analyses
label: opinion
claim: A Dark Room opens with a title, two lines of text, one button; new buttons and text unlock over time so the interface growth mirrors the world; element count grows slowly so players learn each. Risk: minimalism disengages some.

title: Playing to wait: a taxonomy of idle games (CHI 2018)
label: research
claim: Abstract only: analyses play, mechanics, rewards, interactivity, progress rate and user interface of idle games; notes their unusual use of player attention and computer cycles. No interface findings in the abstract.

title: Board Game Arena: tooltips and touchscreen
label: practitioner
claim: Touch users trigger hover tooltips unreliably; proposed fixes: long-press, tap-to-toggle tooltip dismissed by tapping elsewhere, or hiding hover-only tooltips with a hover-capability media query.

title: AppleVis: Kittens Game access
label: verbatim
claim: A VoiceOver user reports browser Kittens Game mouseover text and worker-assign links inaccessible; iOS app better for descriptions.

title: Fix 100vh on mobile viewport
label: practitioner
claim: vh equals the large viewport so 100vh overflows while the mobile address bar shows; dvh tracks the live viewport, svh the smallest. A bottom-pinned bar needs viewport-fit=cover plus env(safe-area-inset-bottom) or env() is zero.

title: NOT FOUND / NULL
label: snippet
claim: Searches for Cookie Clicker / Antimatter Dimensions / Kittens developer accounts of UI growth, Slay the Spire developer reasoning on intent icons, Frostpunk, Darkest Dungeon, gameuidatabase patterns, and primary Apple HIG 44pt / Material 48dp pages returned nothing usable (empty fetch or secondary only). Null, not negative.

title: Apple HIG Accessibility (JSON behind the page)
label: guideline
claim: Table 'Platform / Default control size / Minimum control size': iOS and iPadOS 44x44 pt default, 28x28 pt minimum; macOS 28x28 / 20x20; tvOS 66x66 / 56x56; visionOS 60x60 / 28x28; watchOS 44x44 / 28x28. Also a text-size table: up to 17 pt needs 4.5:1 contrast, 18 pt and bold 3:1.

title: Apple HIG Buttons (JSON behind the page)
label: guideline
claim: 'As a general rule, a button needs a hit region of at least 44x44 pt (in visionOS, 60x60 pt) to ensure that people can select it easily, whether they use a fingertip, a pointer, their eyes, or a remote.'

title: Android: Make apps more accessible
label: guideline
claim: 'For touch interfaces, we recommend that each interactive UI element have a focusable area, or touch target size, of at least 48dpx48dp. Larger is even better.' For precise input (mouse, trackpad) the target can be smaller.

title: Android Accessibility Help: Touch target size
label: guideline
claim: Touch targets include area beyond the visual bounds: an icon may look 24x24dp while padding makes the 48x48dp target. 'Consider making touch targets at least 48x48dp, separated by 8dp of space or more.' Cites the Material Design accessibility guidelines.

title: Hoober 2013 comments: author's later correction
label: verbatim
claim: Hoober, comment of 28 Feb 2017: the reach drawings are 'a bit of a lie because I over-assumed. People touch the center of the screen. More, more quickly, more accurately, and by preference. Not the corners or edges.' 'Please, please everyone ignore those drawings.' Points to later studies that record touch locations directly.

title: Hoober 2017: Design for Fingers, Touch, and People, Part 1
label: research
claim: People shift grip a lot and prefer to view and touch the screen centre. Targets there 'can be smaller, as small as 7 millimeters, while corner target sizes must be about 12 millimeters'; suggested sizes contain only 95% of observed taps. Calls pixel-based standards 'useless' (device pixels bear no relation to human dimensions) and says Google's and Apple's sizes seem based on platform convenience more than human factors. Advice: put dangerous or unrelated items far from others; primary content centre, secondary actions along top and bottom edges.

title: Osmani 2020: Modern Touch-Friendly Design (interview with Hoober)
label: practitioner
claim: Secondary: Hoober's heuristics (people touch the centre, only tap what they see, grip/task/context vary); says avoid the Thumb Zone as a fixed rule; 75% single-thumb figure is misleading next to 49% one-handed grip.

title: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus
label: guideline
claim: Dismissible: 'A mechanism is available to dismiss the additional content without moving pointer hover or keyboard focus'. Hoverable: 'the pointer can be moved over the additional content without the additional content disappearing'. Persistent: 'remains visible until the hover or focus trigger is removed'. The page frames everything around pointer hover and keyboard focus; touch is not mentioned.

title: Fagerholt & Lorentzon 2009, Beyond the HUD (thesis PDF, sections 7-8)
label: research
claim: The thesis's own design space is two axes: fiction (does it exist in the game's fiction?) and spatiality (is it in the 3D game geometry?); an earlier diegesis x spatiality chart was dropped because diegesis proved 'slightly ambiguous' (blood on screen, Mirror's Edge runner vision). Six categories result: non-diegetic (HUD), meta-perception, meta-representation, geometric, diegetic, signifiers. Hypotheses: more competitive games favour clear overlay HUD ('ambiguous information should be avoided' where decisions must be fast); the closer a world is to plausible reality, the more non-diegetic elements hurt; a world that does not hide being artificial tolerates them. FPS-only scope; guidelines untested beyond small user tests.

title: Hodent: Cognitive psychology applied to UX in video games
label: practitioner
claim: Her own definition: usability is 'removing or at least alleviating all the frustrations and confusion the player could experience while playing the game, if they are not intended by design'; the second component is gameflow (from Sweetser and Wyeth, Csikszentmihalyi), a heuristic set for emotion and motivation. A UX framework is used as a checklist of both.

title: Hodent: 5 misconceptions about UX
label: practitioner
claim: 'one of the UX pillar - usability - is about removing friction and unwanted frustration. It's not about distorting the intended experience'; the second pillar is gameflow, 'how enjoyable and fun the game is'. Her blog index later words the pair as 'usability and engage-ability' (Fortnite post); the book's chapters 11 and 12 are titled Usability and Engage-Ability.
